# Reactor and turbine materials
Every rod, blade and stator is printed at the nuclear fabricator in a choice of material, and the material is the whole difference between two rods of the same kind. The short version comes first; the reference tables follow.
[color=#897236][mono]──── [color=#ffdd33][bold]CHOOSING RODS[/bold][/color] ───────────────────────────────────[/mono][/color]
- [color=#a4885c][bold]Fuel rods[/bold][/color] want a high decay chance for heat and a high stimulated emission chance for a reaction that feeds itself. Cerenkite is the gentle starter fuel, uranium the workhorse, plutonium the hottest thing you can print. - [color=#a4885c][bold]Control rods[/bold][/color] want a high interact chance with low emission and low reflection, so neutrons go in and do not come out. Bohrum is the purpose-made choice; steel is the cheap one. - [color=#a4885c][bold]Gas channels[/bold][/color] and [color=#a4885c][bold]heat exchangers[/bold][/color] want thermal transfer above all. The higher the number, the faster heat leaves the fuel, which is the difference between a hot reactor and a melting one. - A high [color=#a4885c][bold]reflection chance[/bold][/color] bounces neutrons back where they came from, which keeps them in the core and out of the room.
[color=#897236][mono]──── [color=#ffdd33][bold]CHOOSING TURBINE PARTS[/bold][/color] ──────────────────────────[/mono][/color]
- A heavier [color=#a4885c][bold]blade[/bold][/color] takes more damage before failing and changes speed more slowly, which makes the turbine easier to hold on its mark. - A better [color=#a4885c][bold]stator[/bold][/color] turns more of the spin into power. It is the single cheapest upgrade to a running plant.
[color=#897236][mono]──── [color=#aa88cc][bold]ROD MATERIAL REFERENCE[/bold][/color] ──────────────────────────[/mono][/color]
Emission and decay chances are for a fresh rod. They drift as the rod is used.
Stimulated emission, decay and reflection only happen to a neutron that first passes the interact chance.
(*) means the value is multiplied by the rod type's neutron cross section, listed under the table; the numbers here assume a cross section of 1.
